holding: For the reasons recorded above, the instant appeal is allowed, subject to payment of costs of Rs.100,000/- by the appellant to the respondent. paragraphs.text: Date of hearing: 05.11.2026. Appellant by: Sheikh Nasir Rafique, Advocate. Respondent by: M/s. Sajid Javed Chohan and Nadia Iffat, Advocates. MUHAMMAD SAJID MEHMOOD SETHI, J.- Through the instant appeal, the appellant has called in question the ex parte judgment and decree dated 05.01.2026 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Jhang, whereby the respondent's suit for recovery of Rs.27,40,000/- under Order XXXVII, C.P.C., instituted on the basis of a cheque, was decreed with costs.

Briefly, the respondent instituted the suit alleging that he had advanced a friendly loan of Rs.27,40,000/- to the appellant on 10.10.2024, against which the appellant issued cheque No.1631708339, drawn on Muslim Commercial Bank, Bhakkar Road Branch, Jhang. The cheque, upon presentation, was returned with a memorandum slip. The appellant filed an application for leave to appear and defend the suit, which was conditionally allowed by the learned Trial Court vide order dated 09.08.2025, subject to furnishing a surety bond equivalent to the suit amount, i.e. Rs.27,40,000/-. The matter was fixed for submission of the surety bond on 22.08.2025 and, thereafter, for orders on 25.08.2025. On the latter date, for non-furnishing of the requisite security, the learned Trial Court recalled its earlier order and dismissed the application for leave to defend. Subsequently, the respondent produced his evidence, including the original cheque (Exh.P-1) and bank memorandum (Exh.P- 2), and the suit was decreed ex parte vide judgment and decree dated 05.01.2026. Hence, the instant appeal.

Learned counsel for the appellant contends that, after conditionally allowing the application for leave to defend, the learned Trial Court afforded only two subsequent dates, i.e. 22.08.2025 and 25.08.2025, for furnishing a surety bond of the substantial amount of Rs.27,40,000/-, and recalled its earlier order on the latter date without affording a reasonable or effective opportunity to comply. He submits that the appellant has a specific defence regarding the circumstances in which the cheque was handed over to a third person as security in connection with a separate dispute and was subsequently misused, raising triable questions requiring evidence. He further assails the impugned judgment as lacking a proper appraisal of the evidence and having been passed merely on the premise that the respondent's evidence remained unchallenged. Reliance is placed upon Naseem Khan v. Sardar Sher Bahadur Khan (PLD 2019 Peshawar 141) and Mian Ejaz Amir v. Haji Muhammad Ibrahim (2023 CLD 534).

Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent maintains that the leave was granted on an unequivocal condition which the appellant failed to comply despite sufficient opportunities. He further contends that the appellant neither sought modification of the condition nor applied for extension of time before the learned Trial Court and, consequently, the respondent became entitled to a decree under the summary procedure prescribed by Order XXXVII, C.P.C.

The questions for determination are whether the recall of conditional leave to defend vide order dated 25.08.2025 was justified and, if not, whether the consequential ex parte decree can be sustained. Order XXXVII, C.P.C. provides a special summary procedure for expeditious adjudication of specified monetary claims founded upon written instruments. Its object is to prevent a defendant from delaying recovery of an apparently liquidated claim through frivolous or sham defences. At the same time, the summary character of the procedure does not dispense with judicial scrutiny where the defendant discloses a bona fide and legally sustainable defence raising a triable issue. Under Rule 3(2) of Order XXXVII, the Court may grant leave to defend either unconditionally or upon such terms as may be considered just, including terms relating to payment into Court, furnishing security, framing and recording of issues or otherwise. The nature of leave and the conditions attached thereto must, therefore, be determined through a judicial exercise of discretion, having regard to the substance of the defence, the conduct of the defendant and the circumstances of the particular case. A condition imposed while granting leave is not an empty formality; once validly imposed, it is binding and must be fulfilled in its true letter and spirit. Its non-fulfilment may render the leave inoperative and expose the defendant to the consequences prescribed by the summary procedure. The question, however, is whether the condition was enforced in a manner consistent with the judicial discretion governing its imposition and enforcement.

The jurisprudence on the subject consistently recognises that the grant of leave to defend is not governed by a mechanical formula. In the case of Mian Ejaz Amir supra, this Court held that the quality and plausibility of the defence constitute the leading consideration in deciding whether leave should be granted conditionally or unconditionally. Even where a defence is plausible, unconditional leave does not follow as an automatic consequence; its strength, substance and the defendant's conduct remain relevant. Equally important, the Court emphasised that while imposing security, it must remain conscious that an onerous condition, if not fulfilled, may result in a decree against a defendant who might otherwise succeed upon establishing his defence. The condition must, therefore, be supported by logical and legally sustainable reasons and must not be arbitrary, oppressive or imposed merely at the asking of the plaintiff.

The same approach emerges from Bashir Ahmed v. Messrs Skyline Lahore (Pvt.) Company through Chief Executive (2012 CLC 1546), wherein this Court collated the guiding principles for grant of leave under Order XXXVII, C.P.C. The nature of the defence determines whether leave should be unconditional or conditional; substantial questions of fact or law, including want of consideration, fraud, jurisdictional objections and other matters requiring inquiry, may justify an opportunity to defend, whereas a weak or doubtful defence may warrant conditional leave. The defendant's conduct, including circumstances suggesting mala fides or an attempt to delay proceedings, is also material. Likewise, in Allah Ditta v. Muhammad Ramzan (2026 CLC 760), this Court reiterated that the discretion to impose conditions must be exercised through independent application of mind and sound judicial reasoning, keeping in view the defence disclosed and the purpose of the summary procedure. The Court disapproved an onerous security condition where its imposition was not supported by an independent assessment of the relevant circumstances. Although the present appeal is not directed against the original condition as such, the underlying principle remains relevant: a judicial condition carrying the consequence of foreclosure of the defence cannot be enforced as a matter of mere formality, without due regard to the circumstances in which compliance is required. The summary procedure must discourage dilatory tactics without converting procedural discipline into an instrument for shutting out a defence which genuinely calls for adjudication.

The order dated 09.08.2025 did not prescribe a separately quantified period for furnishing the surety bond. It fixed 22.08.2025 for framing of issues and submission of the security. On 22.08.2025, the learned Trial Court recorded that the surety bond had not been furnished and fixed 25.08.2025 for orders. On the latter date, both learned counsel were present. The learned Trial Court also recorded that the file had been kept waiting throughout the day, yet the defendant had failed to furnish the bond. It consequently recalled the conditional leave on the ground that the condition precedent had not been fulfilled despite sufficient opportunities. These circumstances cannot be ignored. The appellant had knowledge of the condition and of the date fixed for its fulfilment; it would, therefore, be incorrect to hold that he was afforded no opportunity or was unaware of the consequence of non- compliance. Nevertheless, the record discloses only the initial date fixed for submission of the bond and two subsequent dates, the latter falling merely three days after the former. The security required was equivalent to the entire suit amount of Rs.27,40,000/-, which, depending upon its nature and the means available to the defendant, could require arrangements for a suitable surety and completion of the necessary verification and formalities. The order dated 25.08.2025 records non- compliance and the time for which the file was kept waiting, but does not disclose any consideration of the circumstances preventing compliance, the practical feasibility of arranging the requisite security within the period allowed, or whether a short final opportunity subject to appropriate safeguards could meet the ends of justice. The expression “sufficient opportunities”, in such circumstances, must be examined with reference to the actual time and facilities afforded, rather than treated as conclusive merely because more than one date was fixed. The issue is not whether the appellant could disregard the condition, but whether its immediate enforcement through recall of leave and complete foreclosure of the defence was proportionate to the default in the circumstances reflected by the record.

The respondent's reliance upon the binding principle that a condition attached to leave to defend must be fulfilled is not without substance. In Murtaza Haseeb Textile Mills v. Sitara Chemical Industries (2004 SCMR 882), the Hon'ble Supreme Court recognised that failure to fulfil a condition imposed while granting leave may leave the Court with no option but to proceed in accordance with the summary procedure. However, the factual setting of that case involved a defendant who had been allowed a period of one month to furnish security, unsuccessfully challenged the condition through successive proceedings, furnished property worth substantially less than the amount required, and persisted in non-compliance despite repeated opportunities. The conduct was found to be contumacious. Similarly, in Imdad Ali v. Muhammad Latif (2006 YLR 1450), the defendant had been allowed a definite period of ten days to furnish security, failed to seek extension before its expiry, and subsequently also failed to comply with the direction of the High Court requiring a bank guarantee. The appeal was consequently dismissed in the face of continued non-compliance. In Muhammad Irsalan Faraz v. Habib ul Rehman (2025 CLC 1580), recall of conditional leave was justified in circumstances where the surety bonds furnished by the defendant were found, after inquiry and examination of the relevant record, to be forged. The case involved fraud upon the Court rather than a mere failure to arrange security. These authorities affirm that conditional leave cannot be retained by a defendant who deliberately evades or fraudulently defeats the condition imposed. They do not, however, lay down that every instance of non-compliance, irrespective of its circumstances and the opportunity actually afforded, must invariably result in immediate foreclosure of the defence. The present case is distinguishable in that the record does not disclose successive proceedings intended to frustrate compliance, tender of deficient or fictitious security, forgery, or any express finding of contumacious conduct. Nor was a definite period of ten days or one month prescribed, as in the aforesaid cases. The distinction is not intended to dilute the binding force of a conditional order; it concerns the judicial assessment of the circumstances in which its breach is visited with the most drastic procedural consequence.

The appellant’s failure to seek modification or extension is relevant and cannot be treated as immaterial. The omission is relevant and cannot be treated as immaterial. A defendant who seeks the indulgence of leave to defend is expected to act with diligence and to approach the Court promptly if unable to fulfil a condition imposed upon him. The failure to seek extension may, therefore, weigh against him and justify compensatory costs or other appropriate safeguards. It does not, however, invariably conclude the question whether the opportunity afforded was reasonable, particularly where the consequence is the complete loss of the right to contest the claim. In the cases of Mian Ejaz Amir and Allah Ditta supra, the emphasis upon independent judicial assessment and the practical consequences of onerous conditions makes clear that the Court's responsibility is not exhausted merely because the defendant has remained silent. The principle of proportionality in this context does not confer a right to disregard a condition; it requires the Court to ensure that its enforcement, while preserving the efficacy of the summary procedure, does not result in an avoidable foreclosure of a defence without a fair and effective opportunity to comply. Article 10-A of the Constitution reinforces the requirement of fair process, but it does not override the procedure prescribed by Order XXXVII, C.P.C. Both must be read harmoniously. The present conclusion is confined to the particular sequence of dates, the substantial amount of security, and the absence of a recorded assessment of whether a final, time-bound opportunity could adequately protect the respondent.

The appellant has also raised a defence that the cheque was delivered to a third person as security in connection with a separate dispute and was subsequently misused. Such a plea, if supported by particulars and relevant material, may require inquiry into the circumstances in which the instrument came into the respondent's possession and whether it represented an enforceable liability against the appellant. The principles discussed in Bashir Ahmed supra recognise that pleas involving want of consideration, fraud or circumstances surrounding the issuance of a negotiable instrument may, depending upon their substance and bona fides, raise matters requiring adjudication. At the same time, a bare assertion that a cheque was misused does not, by itself, constitute a plausible defence or entitle a defendant to unconditional leave. The learned Trial Court must examine the application for leave, its supporting affidavit and the material accompanying it to determine whether the plea is bona fide, sufficiently particularised and legally sustainable. The earlier grant of conditional leave cannot be treated as a final judicial finding on the truth of the defence. This Court, likewise, expresses no opinion on whether the cheque was issued as alleged by the respondent or delivered as security in the manner asserted by the appellant. Those matters must remain open for determination on the evidence.

The learned Trial Court recorded the statements of the respondent as PW-1, two alleged witnesses to the transaction as PW-2 and PW-3, and the concerned bank manager as PW-4, besides exhibiting the original cheque (Exh.P-1) and bank memorandum (Exh.P-2). It thereafter decreed the suit substantially on the ground that the respondent's evidence had remained unrebutted and uncross-examined. There can be no cavil with the proposition that evidence which remains unchallenged may carry considerable evidentiary weight. Equally, however, the absence of cross-examination does not automatically render every assertion conclusive or dispense with the Court's duty to assess the evidence in accordance with law. Even in proceedings under Order XXXVII, the consequences contemplated by Rule 2(2), read with Rule 3, must be applied in their proper context. The summary procedure facilitates an expeditious decree where the defendant fails to obtain or retain leave to defend; it does not transform the judicial function into a mechanical exercise. As recognised in Muhammad Irsalan Faraz supra, the Court must apply its mind to the facts and documents before it. In the present case, the learned Trial Court noticed the witnesses and the documents produced, but its discussion does not meaningfully examine the substance of their depositions or the manner in which they establish the alleged advancement of the substantial cash amount of Rs.27,40,000/-. Nor does it explain the evidentiary significance of the cheque and the bank memorandum in relation to the underlying liability. The relevant statutory provisions and presumptions under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, to the extent attracted by the instrument and the facts established, also required consideration. Any such presumption, however, must be applied in accordance with law and does not relieve the Court of examining the foundational facts and the evidence as a whole. The deficiency is not that the respondent produced no evidence, but that the impugned judgment does not disclose a reasoned appraisal of the material relied upon to decree the claim.

An ex parte decree is not liable to be set aside merely because the defendant did not participate in the proceedings, nor does the absence of cross-examination necessarily render the plaintiff's evidence insufficient. The decisive consideration here is that the appellant's exclusion from the evidentiary proceedings flowed directly from the recall of conditional leave. If that recall is found unsustainable in the circumstances, the consequential decree cannot be allowed to stand independently of the procedural foundation upon which it rests. The cumulative effect of the foregoing discussion is that, although the appellant was aware of the security condition and failed to seek its modification or extension, the short interval between the two dates fixed after the conditional order, the substantial amount of security involved, and the absence of a recorded assessment of the feasibility of compliance or the availability of a less drastic safeguard render the immediate recall of leave disproportionate in the peculiar circumstances of this case. This conclusion does not absolve the appellant of his default, nor does it confer upon him an unconditional right to defend the suit. The respondent is equally entitled to protection against delay and to expeditious determination of his claim. The ends of justice would, therefore, be served by restoring the original conditional leave, subject to strict compliance with the security condition and payment of compensatory costs. This course preserves the discipline and summary character of Order XXXVII, C.P.C., while ensuring that a defence which has yet to be judicially assessed is not foreclosed without an effective opportunity of adjudication. The learned Trial Court shall thereafter decide the suit independently, on the basis of the pleadings and evidence, without being influenced by any observation made herein. CONCLUSION

For the reasons recorded above, the instant appeal is allowed, subject to payment of costs of Rs.100,000/- by the appellant to the respondent. The impugned judgment and decree dated 05.01.2026 and the order dated 25.08.2025 are set aside, and the conditional leave granted vide order dated 09.08.2025 is restored. The appellant shall, within twenty (20) days from the date of this judgment, furnish a surety bond of Rs.27,40,000/- to the satisfaction of the learned Trial Court and deposit the aforesaid costs before it for payment to the respondent. Upon compliance with both conditions, the learned Trial Court shall afford the parties an effective opportunity to produce their respective evidence and address arguments, and shall decide the suit through a speaking judgment, strictly on its own merits, within sixty (60) days thereafter. In case of failure to comply with either condition within the stipulated period, the instant appeal shall stand dismissed, without further order, and the order dated 25.08.2025 and judgment and decree dated 05.01.2026 shall stand revived and remain enforceable in accordance with law. The parties shall appear before the learned Trial Court on 26.11.2026, subject to compliance with the above conditions. The observations made herein shall not prejudice either party on the merits of the controversy, which shall be independently determined by the learned Trial Court. A copy of this judgment be transmitted to the learned Trial Court forthwith for information and compliance. (Muhammad Sajid Mehmood Sethi) Judge APPROVED FOR REPORTING Judge *A.H.S.*
